items.informal_name: Almost Every Real Number is Not a Liouville Number for Exponents Greater Than Two
items.informal_description: For almost every real number $x$ with respect to the Lebesgue measure, and for every real number $p > 2$, $x$ is not a Liouville number with exponent $p$. This means that the set of real numbers approximable by rationals to order $p > 2$ has Lebesgue measure zero.

items.informal_name: Liouville Numbers with Exponent Greater Than One Are Irrational
items.type: ∀ {p x : ℝ}, LiouvilleWith p x → 1 < p → Irrational x
items.informal_description: If a real number $ x $ is a Liouville number with exponent $ p > 1 $, then $ x $ is irrational.

Every Liouville number is irrational, i.e., if $ x $ satisfies the Liouville condition that for every natural number $ n $ there exist integers $ a $, $ b $ with $ b > 1 $ such that $ 0 < |x - \frac{a}{b}| < \frac{1}{b^n} $, then $ x $ cannot be expressed as a ratio of integers.

items.informal_name: Equivalence of Liouville Numbers and Liouville Numbers with All Exponents p
items.type: ∀ {x : ℝ}, (∀ (p : ℝ), LiouvilleWith p x) ↔ Liouville x
items.informal_description: A real number $ x $ is a Liouville number if and only if for every positive real number $ p $, there exists a positive constant $ C $ such that for infinitely many natural numbers $ n $, there exists an integer $ m $ with $ x \neq \frac{m}{n} $ and $ \left|x - \frac{m}{n}\right| < \frac{C}{n^p} $.

items.informal_name: Liouville Numbers are LiouvilleWith for Any Exponent
items.type: ∀ {x : ℝ}, Liouville x → ∀ (p : ℝ), LiouvilleWith p x
items.informal_description: If $ x $ is a Liouville number, then for any real number $ p $, $ x $ satisfies the LiouvilleWith condition with exponent $ p $. That is, there exists a positive constant $ C $ such that for infinitely many natural numbers $ n $, there exists an integer $ m $ with $ x \neq \frac{m}{n} $ and $ |x - \frac{m}{n}| < \frac{C}{n^p} $.
A real number $ x $ is called a Liouville number if, for every natural number $ n $, there exist integers $ a $ and $ b $ with $ b > 1 $ such that $ 0 < |x - \frac{a}{b}| < \frac{1}{b^n} $.
For any natural number $m \ge 2$, the Liouville number, defined as the sum of the series $\sum_{i=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{m^{i!}}$, is a transcendental number.

items.informal_name: The Liouville Number Generated by $ m $ is a Liouville Number
items.informal_description: For any natural number $ m \geq 2 $, the Liouville number constructed as the infinite sum $ \sum_{i=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{m^{i!}} $ satisfies the definition of a Liouville number: for every natural number $ n $, there exist integers $ a $ and $ b > 1 $ such that $ 0 < \left|x - \frac{a}{b}\right| < \frac{1}{b^n} $.

items.informal_name: Liouville's Approximation Theorem for Irrational Roots of Integer Polynomials
items.type:
∀ {α : ℝ},
  Irrational α →
    ∀ {f : Polynomial ℤ},
      f ≠ 0 →
        Polynomial.eval α (Polynomial.map (algebraMap ℤ ℝ) f) = 0 →
          ∃ A, 0 < A ∧ ∀ (a : ℤ) (b : ℕ), 1 ≤ (↑b + 1) ^ f.natDegree * (|α - ↑a / (↑b + 1)| * A)
items.informal_description: Let $\alpha$ be an irrational real number and let $f \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$ be a non-zero polynomial such that $f(\alpha) = 0$. Then there exists a positive real number $A$ such that for all integers $a$ and natural numbers $b$, the inequality $1 \leq A \cdot (b + 1)^{\deg(f)} \cdot |\alpha - \frac{a}{b + 1}|$ holds.

A real number $ x $ satisfies the Liouville condition with exponent $ 1 $, meaning there exists a positive constant $ C $ such that for infinitely many natural numbers $ n $, there exists an integer $ m $ with $ x \neq \frac{m}{n} $ and $ \left|x - \frac{m}{n}\right| < \frac{C}{n} $.

items.informal_name: Liouville numbers with exponent $ p > 1 $ are not integers
items.type: ∀ {p x : ℝ}, LiouvilleWith p x → 1 < p → ∀ (m : ℤ), x ≠ ↑m
items.informal_description: If $ x $ is a Liouville number with exponent $ p > 1 $, then $ x $ is not equal to any integer $ m $. This follows from the definition of Liouville numbers requiring arbitrarily good rational approximations, which integers cannot satisfy for exponents greater than 1.
